Two later movements, the Stone-Campbell Restoration and the Holiness movement, grew directly out of this ferment.

prose_changes.old: In 1796 a Norwegian farmer's son named Hans Nielsen Hauge had a religious experience while working in his father's field, and set out on foot to tell people about it. Which was against the law, because Norway's Conventicle Act reserved religious meetings to the parish clergy. He wrote thirty-three books and tracts, walked thousands of miles, and founded mills, paper works and trading businesses to support the network of "friends" that grew around him; the state answered by arresting him in 1804 and keeping him in prison and under prosecution for most of the following decade. The movement long outlasted the man: after his death in 1824 the friends' societies went on meeting and trading, and in 1842 the Conventicle Act itself was repealed.
